statement: Two equal rectangles, each 5 cm long and 3 cm wide, are joined along their long sides to make one bigger rectangle. How far is it all the way around the bigger rectangle?

choices.misconception: I added one long side and one short side of the big rectangle, 5 + 6, and stopped.
I gave the distance around just one of the small rectangles.
I joined them along their short sides, which makes a rectangle 10 cm long and 3 cm wide.
I added the distances around both small rectangles, counting the sides that are now hidden inside.

hints: Draw the two rectangles joined along their long sides.
Work out the length and width of the new, bigger rectangle from the drawing. Sides that touch are now inside, so they are not part of the distance around.
The big rectangle is still 5 cm long, but it is 3 + 3 = 6 cm wide. Go round it: 5, 6, 5, 6.

solutions.reliable: Joining along the 5 cm sides stacks the rectangles, so the big rectangle is 5 cm long and $3 + 3 = 6$ cm wide. All the way around is $5 + 6 + 5 + 6 = 22$ cm. The idea to keep: when shapes are joined, the touching sides go inside and stop counting.
solutions.elegant: Each small rectangle measures 16 cm around, so 32 cm for both. Joining hides one 5 cm side from each rectangle, so take away $5 + 5 = 10$ cm: $32 - 10 = 22$ cm.

whyOnTest: Joining shapes hides the touching sides, and which sides touch changes the answer, so drawing the joined shape is the reliable step.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
